title: The NRI's Guide to Australia — Great Barrier Reef, Cricket at the MCG, and 900,000 Indians Who Got There First
excerpt: Melbourne and Sydney have Little Indias that rival Southall or Jackson Heights. The diaspora is booming Down Under.
body:
## Why Australia?

Australia is where India's diaspora is booming — over 900,000 Indian-born Australians make it the country's largest source of new migrants. Melbourne and Sydney have Little Indias that rival Southall or Jackson Heights. For NRIs in America visiting family who moved Down Under, or for those looking for a destination that combines adventure, urban culture, and natural wonders at a scale that dwarfs everything else, Australia delivers like few places can. The Great Barrier Reef, the Outback, Sydney Harbour, and the world's most liveable cities are all packed into a single country. Yes, it is far. Yes, it is worth it.

## Top Experiences

**1. Great Barrier Reef, Queensland** — The largest living structure on earth stretches over 2,300 km. Snorkel or dive from Cairns or the Whitsunday Islands. Take a scenic helicopter flight for the aerial perspective. The reef is under climate stress — visit now while it is still magnificent.

**2. Sydney Harbour: Opera House & Bridge** — Walk across the Harbour Bridge or climb it (BridgeClimb, $200–350 AUD). Take a ferry to Manly Beach. Watch a performance at the Opera House — the building is more impressive inside than out. Circular Quay at sunset is Sydney at its best.

**3. Great Ocean Road, Victoria** — One of the world's greatest coastal drives. The Twelve Apostles limestone stacks, Loch Ard Gorge, and the surf town of Torquay are the highlights. Drive from Melbourne — it is a 3–4 hour trip one way, or better as an overnight.

**4. Uluru (Ayers Rock), Northern Territory** — The sacred red monolith at sunrise or sunset is a spiritual experience. Climbing is now prohibited (and was always culturally inappropriate). Take the base walk, learn from Aboriginal guides, and watch the Field of Light installation at night.

**5. Melbourne: Coffee, Laneways & Cricket** — Melbourne is Australia's culture and food capital. Explore the street-art-covered laneways, drink flat whites in hidden cafés, and watch cricket at the MCG — the cathedral of the sport. The Indian community in Harris Road (Dandenong) is thriving.

## Getting There

From the US, direct flights to Sydney on United (SFO, 15 hours), Qantas (LAX/DFW, 15–17 hours), and Delta (LAX, seasonal). Melbourne is usually one stop via Sydney, Auckland, or Singapore. From India, direct flights from Delhi and Mumbai to Sydney and Melbourne on Air India and Qantas (11–13 hours). Internal flights on Qantas, Virgin Australia, and Jetstar connect the major cities — Sydney to Melbourne is 1.5 hours, Sydney to Cairns is 3 hours.

## Where to Stay

Sydney: Stay in The Rocks or Circular Quay for harbour proximity. Darling Harbour for families. Bondi for beach vibes. Four Seasons and Park Hyatt for luxury, Travelodge and Ibis for budget. Melbourne: Southbank or CBD. Crown Towers for luxury, QT Melbourne for design. Cairns: Pullman Reef Hotel Casino or Shangri-La for reef trip access. Budget throughout Australia: YHA hostels are excellent and clean ($30–50 AUD per night). Airbnb is popular and often 40% cheaper than hotels.

## Food & the Desi Connection

Australia's Indian food scene is genuinely excellent — Harris Road in Dandenong (Melbourne) and Harris Park in Sydney are full-scale Indian suburbs with restaurants, sweet shops, and grocery stores matching anything in New Jersey or the Bay Area. Lakemba in Sydney has outstanding Sri Lankan and South Indian food. Beyond Indian cuisine, Australia's food culture is multicultural — try a meat pie, fish and chips at Bondi, Vietnamese pho in Melbourne's Richmond, and the flat white (an Australian invention). Vegetarians do well in Australia's health-conscious food scene. Melbourne is consistently ranked among the world's best food cities.

## NRI Tips

Indian passport holders need a Visitor visa (subclass 600) — apply online through the Australian Immigration website, processed in days to weeks. US citizens need an ETA (subclass 601) — approved almost instantly online. Currency is the Australian Dollar (AUD) — roughly $0.65 USD. Australia is expensive — budget $150–300 AUD per day. Tipping is not expected (a welcome relief for NRIs used to American tipping culture). Driving is on the left side — consider whether you are comfortable with it before renting a car. The distances are enormous — Sydney to Melbourne is 9 hours by car. Fly between cities unless doing a dedicated road trip. Sun safety is critical — Australia has the highest skin cancer rates in the world. SPF 50+, hat, and rash guard for beaches. Best months: September to November (spring) and March to May (autumn) for moderate temperatures. December to February is summer — hot but perfect for beaches.
author: Diaspora Desk
